main_argument_chains.claim: Earlier event locations can rank a bounded next-crime search area when offender linkage and nonrandom spatial behavior are plausible.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the ranked area only after case linkage, historical accuracy, and resource capacity are checked.

main_argument_chains.claim: Recency weighting can adapt spatial fields to moving behavior.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Calibrate the recency rule inside rolling origins before treating it as reliable for a case.

main_argument_chains.claim: Simple equal-weight fusion can be numerically competitive without being statistically dominant.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Report numeric rank and inferential support separately and avoid post-selection claims.

main_argument_chains.claim: Operational usefulness must be case-specific rather than inferred from the corpus mean.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Abstain or fall back to traditional investigation when historical case diagnostics fail.

warnings.warning: Hit score counts only sectors strictly above the held-out sector and does not specify tie ordering, so tied fields can receive optimistically small search fractions.
Hit score is denominator-sensitive; the twice-maximum-distance search square is reproducible but heuristic and lacks size, shape, and grid-resolution sensitivity.
The inverse-distance centralization score is singular if a sector representative coincides with the focal point.
The harmonic mean of two-dimensional coordinates is mathematically ambiguous and can be unstable at zero or across signed coordinate values.
Linear decay can become negative, so the quantity is not a probability unless truncated or explicitly treated only as a ranking score.
The claim that exponential-decay constants do not affect hit-score ranking is generally false because changing gamma can reorder sums of several exponential contributions.
Temporal normalization uses t_n rather than explicitly t_n-t_1, making the formula dependent on how the time origin is encoded.
With k=0.1 and t_1=0, the last-to-first temporal weight ratio is 11 rather than the stated approximately ten.
The fixed temporal offset k=0.1 has no calibration, uncertainty, or sensitivity analysis.
The random baseline assigns independent random sector values, but reproducibility seeds and tie behavior are not reported.
The statement that all proposed methods significantly outperform random does not name the test, p-value, multiplicity handling, or exact inferential unit.
Figure 5 uses 50 percent confidence intervals without explaining the unconventional level or displaying sample sizes by history length.
The corpus contains only nine heterogeneous sequences and 124 crimes, with large imbalance from 6 to 40 crimes per sequence.
Performance varies sharply by offender; the Columbus serial rapist score is worse than random even though aggregate performance is favorable.
Aggregation weights, inclusion choices, and decay calibration are developed and evaluated on the same small corpus, creating tuning-selection optimism.
The meaning of the Table 2 confidence column is not explicit in the header; prose implies it is a plus-or-minus half-width.
The exponential calibration gamma=sqrt(2/delta_bar) is asserted through a desired mean-distance relationship without a full derivation under the pooled field.
The cost-resource recommendation remains qualitative and does not measure software cost, investigator training cost, search capacity, or error consequences.
The paper sometimes calls lower-is-better hit score an accuracy value, which can invert the intuitive direction for readers.
Reference text contains source-level spelling errors and one incomplete citation, limiting bibliographic reproducibility.

visualization_dispositions.analytical_purpose: Shows the complete task-method-metric-result-boundary chain on one competition summary sheet.
Turns model validity into linkage, historical accuracy, and resource-capacity checks.
Keeps omitted geography, omitted offender features, and human comparison visible beside the recommendation.
Confirms full route and absence of an appendix.
Audits nine sequences, 124 crimes, and the extreme offender-specific spread from 0.020 to 0.517.
Defines the square grid sectors and cell-resolution interface used by every ranking model.
Contrasts a single centroid hotspot with an exponential field concentrated around all observed crimes.
Shows how temporal weighting moves the field toward the recent end of an eastward sequence.
Compares aggregate hit scores for random and all individual models with uncertainty bars.
Shows unstable hit score by number of observed crimes with 50 percent confidence intervals.
Provides exact mean hit scores and 95 percent confidence half-widths for ten models.
Shows the pure circle-center endpoint of the opinion-pool weight sweep.
Shows intermediate hotspot movement and shape under 0.25/0.75 and 0.50/0.50 weights.
Shows the transition to a pure exponential-decay field.
Compares one-standard-deviation rectangle and ellipse search regions for Peter Sutcliffe.
Maps the Sutcliffe event locations on recognizable geography with a physical scale.
Shows the Bradford-centered temporal exponential-decay risk field and secondary Manchester hotspot.
